note: All scenarios are fictional (Northwind Logistics). Each option carries its own feedback. 'objective' refers to objectives in docs/design/learning-objectives.md.

items.stem: A colleague says: "The assistant gave me the exact delivery date, so it must have looked it up in our order system." What is the best response?

options.text: "Yes, it must be connected to our systems — otherwise it couldn't know the date."
options.feedback: Not unless a tool was explicitly connected. A general assistant predicts likely text; it has no live access to Northwind's order system. Treating a predicted date as a looked-up fact is exactly the Module 1 trap.

options.text: "It predicted a likely-sounding date from patterns in text. Unless a tool is connected, it can't see our systems — so check the date in the order system before using it."
options.feedback: Correct. Prediction, not lookup. The date is plausible text, not a fact from the system — verify it like any unconfirmed claim.

options.text: "The AI is always right about logistics topics — it was trained on lots of shipping data."
options.feedback: Training data gives it plausible patterns, not current facts about your orders. Fluent and confident is not evidence of truth.

options.text: "It doesn't matter — the customer only needs a quick answer."
options.feedback: It matters: a wrong date creates a promise Northwind cannot keep. Quick and wrong is the most expensive kind of answer (Module 2).

items.stem: Which of these Northwind tasks is the BEST fit for a general AI assistant, used as taught in Module 1?

options.text: Calculating the exact delivery cost for a 40 kg pallet to Rotterdam
options.feedback: Poor fit: exact arithmetic plus a live tariff table. Use the pricing tool; language models predict number-shaped text.

options.text: Drafting a first reply to a complaint about a late delivery
options.feedback: Correct. Text drafting with human checks is the strongest use case — you verify names, dates and promises before sending (Module 2).

options.text: Deciding which of three applicants gets an interview
options.feedback: Poor fit: a decision about people stays with a human (Module 4), and AI ranking risks unfair bias.

options.text: Forecasting next month's delivery volume
options.feedback: Poor fit for a general assistant: forecasting needs real historical data and a proper tool. A chatbot produces a confident-sounding guess.

items.stem: Your team lead asks the assistant to "decide which driver should get a formal warning" based on delay statistics. What is the strongest reason to push back?

options.text: The assistant might use too many words in its explanation.
options.feedback: Length is not the issue. The problem is that a formal warning affects a person's job — that decision must be owned by a human.

options.text: A formal warning affects a person's job, so a human must make and own that decision — an AI suggestion cannot be accountable for it.
options.feedback: Correct — that is the affected-person test from Module 4. AI may summarize the statistics; the decision and its accountability stay human.

options.text: The assistant is new, so we should wait a month before using it for anything.
options.feedback: Waiting does not fix the category. For decisions about people, the human-decides rule applies no matter how mature the tool is.

options.text: Only managers are allowed to use AI tools at Northwind.
options.feedback: That is not the rule in this program — and it is not the reason. The reason is the affected person, not who may click the tool.

items.stem: An AI-drafted reply to a customer contains: "As discussed last Tuesday, your replacement parcel is already on its way and will arrive tomorrow before noon." You have no record of any conversation last Tuesday. What is this sentence?

options.text: A factual error plus an unverifiable claim — both must be fixed or removed before sending.
options.feedback: Correct. "As discussed last Tuesday" asserts a conversation you cannot confirm (unverifiable), and "arrives tomorrow before noon" is a delivery promise you have not checked (unverified). Module 2, steps 1–2.

options.text: A fine sentence — fluent text is usually right.
options.feedback: Fluency is not evidence. Both claims are unverified, and one references a meeting that may never have happened.

options.text: Only a style problem — the sentence is too long.
options.feedback: The problem is truth, not length. Shorten it only after you have made every claim verifiable.

options.text: A data-privacy problem — you pasted personal data.
options.feedback: This sentence's problem is verification, not pasting. (Pasting is Module 3 — a different check on the same job aid.)

items.stem: An AI-drafted internal memo cites "the 2023 European Parcel Handling Directive, published by the European Logistics Board" to justify a packaging change. You have never heard of either. What do you do?

options.text: Include it — a directive with an official-sounding name is a safe citation.
options.feedback: Official-sounding names are exactly what fabricated sources look like. Invented organizations and reports are a standard failure mode.

options.text: Check whether the directive and the European Logistics Board exist and say this; if you cannot verify them, remove the citation and the claim it supports.
options.feedback: Correct — Module 2, step 3. Open the source; if it does not exist or does not say this, the claim goes too. No source you would show your manager = no source.

options.text: Replace it with a different, more famous law without checking.
options.feedback: Swapping one unverified citation for another keeps the problem. The check is the point, not the name.

options.text: Ask the AI to confirm that the directive exists — if it confirms, keep it.
options.feedback: The AI that predicted the citation will happily predict a confirmation. Verification means an independent source, not the author vouching for itself.

items.stem: You are about to send an AI-drafted summary of a delivery report. Using the Verify-before-you-send job aid, which comes FIRST?

options.text: Check every number in the summary against the source report.
options.feedback: Correct — though all five checks matter, the job aid order starts with claims and numbers: AI summaries most often corrupt figures, and a confident wrong number is invisible in a meeting.

options.text: Format the summary nicely for the meeting.
options.feedback: Polish comes last — formatting a wrong summary just makes the wrong numbers more persuasive.

options.text: Send it — the AI summarized the document, so the numbers are from it.
options.feedback: Summaries are where numbers get invented or quietly changed (Joris's case in Module 2). "From the document" is exactly what must be checked.

options.text: Add a disclaimer that the numbers might be wrong.
options.feedback: A disclaimer does not fix a wrong number — it delegates your check to the reader. Verify or remove.

items.stem: You want the assistant to draft a reply and paste this prompt: "Draft a reply for Mrs. Petra Weber about order NW-88123 at Musterstraße 12, Münster." Under the Northwind traffic-light rule (Module 3), what is this paste?

options.text: Permitted — an order number is not secret.
options.feedback: The order number alone would be fine, but with a name and address it identifies a specific person — that combination is prohibited.

options.text: Restricted — it is internal information, so use an approved tool.
options.feedback: Restricted is for internal, non-personal information. A name + address + order number is personal data — prohibited in any external tool, approved or not.

options.text: Prohibited — name + address + order number together identify a specific person. Describe the issue type instead: "a complaint about a late delivery".
options.feedback: Correct. Identifiability is the trigger. The AI does not need the identity to draft good text — you add it back from the system in the reply.

options.text: Prohibited, but only because the address is a home address.
options.feedback: Close, but the reason is broader: name + any address + order number identifies the person. Partial card digits, complaint texts, CVs — all prohibited for the same reason.

items.stem: Which of these pastes into a company-approved AI tool is PERMITTED under the traffic-light rule?

options.text: "In May, 13% of parcels to Münster were delayed." (an anonymized aggregate from a report)
options.feedback: Correct — no person is identifiable, so it is permitted. Anonymized aggregates are the safe way to give the model context.

options.text: A customer's email including their complaint and phone number
options.feedback: Prohibited: the text identifies the person and their situation. Describe the issue type instead.

options.text: An applicant's CV, to "summarize strengths and weaknesses"
options.feedback: Prohibited on two counts: a CV is personal data (Module 3), and ranking or judging people is an oversight question (Module 4).

options.text: Unannounced 2027 contract pricing, pasted into your personal chatbot account
options.feedback: Two failures: unannounced pricing is restricted (approved tools only), and a personal account is never an approved tool for internal information.

items.stem: Yesterday, a colleague pasted a customer's name and address into a personal chatbot account. It is now the next morning. What should happen first?

options.text: Delete the chat quietly — if nobody saw it, there is no incident.
options.feedback: Hiding turns a small incident into a serious one. Deletion does not undo the processing that already happened outside Northwind's control.

options.text: Stop using that chat and report it today, so the team lead and the data protection officer can decide the next steps.
options.feedback: Correct — Module 3's "too late" path: stop → report the same day → lead and DPO take over. Reporting fast is always the right answer.

options.text: Wait to see whether the customer complains.
options.feedback: Waiting transfers the cost of the mistake to the person affected. The report does not depend on anyone noticing.

options.text: Paste the same data into the approved tool instead — problem solved.
options.feedback: That adds a second uncontrolled copy. The original exposure still needs reporting and containment.

items.stem: HR wants to paste 240 CVs into the assistant, have it score each 1–100, and invite the top 20 to interviews. What is the correct call?

options.text: Fine, as long as a human sends the invitations afterwards.
options.feedback: The human only sees the survivors of the scoring pattern. When a filter removes 220 of 240 people, the "human decision" happens inside a funnel that may be biased.

options.text: AI may inform (draft interview questions, summarize requirements), but scoring and ranking people is a decision about people — humans screen, and any AI screening idea goes to the DPO and HR leadership as a formal decision.
options.feedback: Correct — the affected-person test plus the escalation path. Sofia's scenario in Module 4: name the risk, keep the goal, move the decision to the right owner.

options.text: Fine, because the model was trained on millions of CVs and is therefore objective.
options.feedback: Trained on human text means it can repeat human bias — systematically and at scale. "Objective" is the exact opposite of what to assume.

options.text: Prohibited — no AI tool may ever be used in any HR process.
options.feedback: Too broad. AI may inform HR work (drafting questions, templates, summaries). The line is: it does not decide about people.

items.stem: The AI assistant suggests declining a customer's damage claim with a firm refusal. The claim is borderline. Who should decide whether to send the refusal?

options.text: The assistant — it has processed thousands of similar claims.
options.feedback: This changes something for a person (their money). The affected-person test says a human decides; the assistant may inform.

options.text: A named human at Northwind reviews the borderline claim and owns the decision; the AI's suggestion is one input.
options.feedback: Correct. For decisions affecting a person, a named human owns the outcome. The person affected can then ask someone — and someone is actually accountable.

options.text: Whoever is nearest the printer at the time.
options.feedback: Someone must own it — but accountability means a named, appropriate owner, not an accident of geography.

options.text: The customer — they can appeal the AI's decision if they disagree.
options.feedback: Putting the appeal burden on the affected person inverts the responsibility. Northwind decides, humanly, first.

items.stem: An AI tool recommends delivery routes that quietly skip drivers' legally required rest breaks, saving 6% in fuel. Which high-risk signals apply, and what is the move?

options.text: No signals — it is just route optimization, a normal AI task.
options.feedback: It affects people's safety and breaks the law — that is nearly every high-risk signal at once. "Just optimization" is how hazardous recommendations get shipped.

options.text: Signals: affects persons (driver safety), scale (every route), legal/safety dimension. The move: do not act on it; escalate immediately to the responsible manager.
options.feedback: Correct — Module 4's signals 1, 2 and 5. Safety and law make this a hard stop, not a cost-benefit discussion at the dispatch desk.

options.text: One signal (it affects drivers), so a quick team chat about it is enough.
options.feedback: Under-counted and under-escalated. Multiple signals stacked (safety + scale + law) mean a formal escalation, not a chat.

options.text: Signals: it affects fuel costs. The move: ask the AI to find a cheaper route.
options.feedback: That optimizes the wrong thing — the illegal part stays. Name the human harm and the legal dimension, and escalate.
